title: Bedtime Stories
full_review:
Parents will find little to concern them in the reasonably entertaining adventure comedy "Bedtime Stories" (Disney). But, though unobjectionable -- some mildly crude gags aside -- this Adam Sandler vehicle, which affirms perseverance and family unity, relies on humor clearly geared to the grade-school set.

Sandler plays hardworking but underappreciated hotel handyman Skeeter Bronson. As the narrating voice of Skeeter's deceased father, Marty (Jonathan Pryce), informs us, the luxurious hostelry that employs him was once a modest motel built and run by Marty himself when Skeeter was a boy.

But Marty had no head for figures and, with the concern on the verge of bankruptcy, sold out to ambitious British businessman Barry Nottingham (Richard Griffiths), who promised that Skeeter would have a role in his future establishment.

Currently blocking Skeeter's rise to greater responsibilities is smarmy manager Kendall (Guy Pearce), who, in addition to toadying to Barry's eccentric germ phobia, is also dating his glamorous, paparazzi-pursued daughter, Violet (Teresa Palmer), for whose affections Skeeter would like to rival him.

Skeeter's luck begins to change when his school-principal sister, Wendy (Courteney Cox), asks him to watch her son, Patrick (Jonathan Morgan Heit), and daughter Bobbi (Laura Ann Kesling) while she's out of town on job interviews. At a loss to keep the kids (who aren't allowed to watch TV) entertained, Skeeter spins fanciful yarns based on his own life, but set in the Middle Ages, the Old West and outer space.

When these tales magically begin to shape reality, Skeeter tries to use them to defeat Kendall in a competition to choose a theme for the new hotel Barry is building. The romantic focus of his stories, meanwhile, shifts from Violet to Wendy's down-to-earth friend, Jill (Keri Russell), who's sharing the baby-sitting duties.

The fantasy sequences are the strongest draw in director Adam Shankman's warmhearted offering, along with Pryce's narration and a fine performance from Russell Brand as Skeeter's quirky friend and co-worker, Mickey.

"Bedtime Stories" takes a break from comedy to deal with the children's desertion by their father and the pain inflicted by his divorce from Wendy. Skeeter does his best to fill this void with avuncular affection, and eventually reconciles his temperamental differences with Wendy as well.

The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.
